chapter: Miles Davis stories and what jazz means
title: Jazz and fear of sexuality: a publisher's reaction in 1955; records in the Army
summary: Gil says objections to jazz are a fear of sexuality. A publisher called his arrangement dirty in 1955, and soldiers objected to his records.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Sounds funny, but it's basically a fear of sexuality. All of it. I remember one time I took an arrangement up to a publisher ( for an album ?) called 'Easy Things to Remember'. Rodgers and Hart tune. 'Easy Things to Remember'. I had it written like this. (PLAYS PIANO). Kind of like this. (PLAYS PIANO).

He said, 'that's the dirtiest thing I ever heard. It reminds me,' this is a man from Boston, I was flabbergasted, he said, 'that's the dirtiest thing I ever heard. It reminds me of a dose of clap.' Up in Chapell Music. A big high class music company here in New York. This was twenty years ago.

Twenty years ago. And that was 1955. typical I found out. Of course in the Army I had a hard time. A lot of people didn't like my albums, my records. I carried a case of, I used to have a little metal case full of 78s.
Most of all those albums were of Duke Louis Armstrong. Ellington, I had some very, very close calls with some soldiers, some draftees. (They couldn't stand it so dirty) (VOICE FADES OUT).
They used to refer to it as that, nigger music, don't play that nigger music around here.
